newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaiti men flock to elect new parliament.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaiti men flock to elect new parliament.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Kuwaiti men voted on Monday to elect the second parliament since the 1991 Gulf War while hundreds of women held gatherings to demand political rights.
Unofficial estimates put the turnout at more than 75 percent of the 107,000 Kuwaiti men eligible to vote.
Kuwait state television showed police officers closing the main gates of polling stations on time at eight p.m. (1700 GMT) as the 12-hour voting period passed without incidents.

Hundreds of women held three gatherings near polling stations to demand the right to vote. Some women waved banners reading: "Equality now"; "Empowering women empowers the nation"; and "We demand equality and justice".

Police and military personnel, Kuwaitis under 21, those naturalised less than 20 years ago and women -- over 50 percent of Kuwaitis -- cannot vote. Only a seventh of 700,000 Kuwaitis can vote in the only parliament poll in a Gulf Arab state.
Polling stations were crowded in the evening with white- robed men. Candidates said they expected the turn out to exceed 80 percent.

Concerns over perceived renewed Iraqi threats and economic reforms to streamline government spending and balance the budget are the main issues in the election but many Kuwaitis are closely watching the outcome in two districts.

In the fourth district many Sunni Moslem Kuwaitis, slightly more than half of the 3,194 voters, are opposed to the controversial Hussein Qalaf, a Shi'ite scholar who traces his family tree to the Prophet Mohammad, voters said.
"Sunni Kuwaitis don't want to see a turbaned Shi'ite scholar entering the assembly," said one analyst. Shi'ites are about 25 percent of Kuwaitis.
Qalaf supporters told Reuters before polls closed that they were confident their candidate had won.
Results are expected to be announced early on Tuesday.

Kuwaitis are also watching the well-to-do third district where former finance minister Jassim al-Kharafi, a member of one of Kuwait's richest families which has global holdings, is running for one of the 50 elected parliament seats.
Analysts say if Kharafi wins he could pose a serious threat to parliament speaker and veteran opposition leader Ahmad al- Saadoun in his bid to get re-elected as president of the camber.
Saadoun is widely expected to win in his constituency.

Many of the Islamist, liberal, independent, pan-Arab nationalist and pro-government candidates set up tents around polling stations to lure voters in with a free lunch and a last chance to influence their final decision.
No incidents were reported in the relaxed voting atmosphere despite fierce election campaigns and bitter exchanges in recent weeks.

"This is the nature of democracy in Kuwait...Election campaigns are hot but on election day things are calm and the competition is honest," said candidate Abdulla al-Roumi who is seeking re-election in the fourth district.
The government, headed by the country's Crown Prince Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah, is due to resign in the next few days.
But even if the new parliament is once again dominated by opposition figures Sheikh Saad is widely expected to form and head the next cabinet.

The last parliament opened probes into alleged corruption and claims of poor government management before Iraq's 1990 invasion. Citing security concerns, parliament was dissolved in 1986, at the height of the nearby Iran-Iraq war.
